title: Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) — Management Guide
content:
## Fall Armyworm (FAW) — Spodoptera frugiperda

Fall Armyworm is an invasive pest that arrived in Africa in 2016. It is now the #1 pest threat to maize across Sub-Saharan Africa.

### Identification

**Egg stage:** White to cream egg masses on leaves, covered with greyish scales from the moth's body.

**Larvae (caterpillar stage — the damaging stage):**
- 6 larval instars (stages), 2–3cm to 4.5cm long
- Distinctive inverted Y-shaped suture on head
- 4 dots arranged in a square on 8th abdominal segment (key ID feature)
- Early instars: feed on leaf surface leaving transparent 'windows'
- Late instars: bore into the whorl (heart of the plant) leaving ragged holes and frass (sawdust-like excrement)

**Damage:**
- Young plants: feeding in whorl causes 'dead heart'
- Older plants: cob attack — larvae bore into cob silk and grain

### Scouting

Scout twice weekly during V1–V6 (first 6 leaf) stage:
- Check 25 plants at 5 locations in the field
- Action threshold: 20% of plants infested with live larvae

### Control Options

**Biological (preferred early season):**
- Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray into the whorl: Dipel, Agree, Xentari at 500g/ha
- Neem extract (Azadirachtin): spray into whorl, 5ml/L

**Chemical (when >20% infestation):**
- Emamectin benzoate (Coragen, Steward): 200ml/ha — most effective against FAW
- Lufenuron (Match): 500ml/ha — insect growth regulator
- Chlorpyrifos (Dursban): 500ml/ha — effective but toxic; use PPE
- Spinetoram (Radiant): 250ml/ha

**Application tip:** Direct spray into the whorl (heart of plant), not on leaves. Best time: morning or evening when larvae are active.

**Resistance note:** Do NOT use pyrethroids alone — FAW has developed resistance in many African populations. Rotate chemical classes each season.
content_sw:
## Viwavi vya Jeshi (Fall Armyworm)

Viwavi vya jeshi walifika Afrika mwaka 2016. Ni tishio kubwa kwa mahindi.

### Kutambua

- Viwavi wakubwa: wana mstari wa Y kwenye kichwa
- Vidokezo 4 vilivyopangwa mraba kwenye sehemu ya mwisho ya mwili
- Uharibifu: matundu kwenye mstari wa mahindi na kinyesi (mchanga wa mbao)

### Kudhibiti

**Kibiolojia:**
- Dawa ya Bt (Dipel): ml 500/hekta ndani ya mstari
- Dawa ya neem: ml 5 kwa lita 1 ya maji

**Kemikali (>20% ya mimea imeathirika):**
- Emamectin benzoate (Coragen): ml 200/hekta — ufanisi mkubwa
- Nyunyizia kwenye mstari wa mahindi, si kwenye majani

title: Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN) — Detection and Response
content:
## Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN)

MLN is caused by a combination of Maize Chlorotic Mottle Virus (MCMV) and a cereal potyvirus (usually SCMV). It is a **notifiable disease in Kenya** — you must report suspected cases to the Ministry of Agriculture.

### Symptoms (progression)

1. **Early (V3–V6):** Pale yellow mottling/mosaic pattern on lower leaves, starting at leaf base and tips
2. **Mid (V7–V10):** Chlorosis spreads; small, poorly filled cobs develop; leaves dry prematurely from edges
3. **Severe:** Plant death before or after tasseling; total crop loss

### How MLN differs from Nitrogen Deficiency

| Feature | Nitrogen Deficiency | MLN |
|---------|---------------------|-----|
| Pattern | V-shaped yellowing from tip down midrib | Mosaic/mottled pattern |
| Progression | Slow, responds to fertilizer in 2 weeks | Rapid, does NOT respond to fertilizer |
| Cob fill | Normal if treated | Poorly filled or empty |
| Plant death | Rarely kills plant | Can kill entire field |
| Spread | Not contagious | Spreads plant-to-plant via thrips/aphids |

### Spread

MLN is spread by:
- **Thrips** (Frankliniella williamsi) — primary vector of MCMV
- **Aphids** (Rhopalosiphum maidis) — vector of SCMV
- **Infected seed** — plant certified seed only

### Management

**Prevention (most important):**
- Plant MLN-tolerant/resistant varieties: DK777, Afya, WS403, H614D MLN-T, SC403
- Use certified seed — not own-saved seed
- Rogue (remove and bury/burn) infected plants immediately
- Control thrips and aphids: Dimethoate or Imidacloprid at early sign
- Do not plant maize after maize in MLN-affected areas — rotate with legumes

**If MLN confirmed:**
- Report to local Ministry of Agriculture extension officer
- Do NOT harvest for seed
- Destroy affected crop: bury or burn (do not compost)
- Rotate with beans, soybean, or vegetables for at least one season
content_sw:
## Ugonjwa wa Lethal Necrosis (MLN)

MLN ni ugonjwa wa virusi ambao unaathiri mahindi. Ni **ugonjwa wa kutangazwa Kenya** — taarifa kwa afisa kilimo wako.

### Dalili

1. Mwanzo: Rangi ya mosaic (madoa ya njano) kwenye majani ya chini
2. Kati: Majani yanakauka; masungu mabaya; chipsi chache
3. Kali: Mmea unakufa kabla ya kuiva

### Tofauti na Upungufu wa Nitrojeni

Upungufu wa nitrojeni: unaitikia mbolea baada ya wiki 2. MLN: HAITIKII mbolea.

### Kuzuia

- Panda aina zinazostahimili MLN: DK777, Afya, WS403
- Tumia mbegu zilizoidhinishwa tu
- Ng'oa na uchome mimea iliyoathirika mara moja

title: Tomato Diseases — Late Blight, Bacterial Wilt, TYLCV
content:
## Major Tomato Diseases in East Africa

### 1. Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)

**Symptoms:** Water-soaked spots on leaves, turning brown-black with white fungal growth on underside in humid conditions. Fruit shows brown firm rot. Spreads extremely fast in cool, wet conditions.

**Conditions favoring it:** Temperature 10–25°C, >80% humidity, prolonged leaf wetness. Most destructive in Kenya/Tanzania highlands during long rains.

**Control:**
- Preventive sprays: Mancozeb (Dithane M45) 2.5kg/ha every 7–10 days; begin before first symptom
- Curative: Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold) 2.5kg/ha; Cymoxanil + Mancozeb (Curzate) 1.5kg/ha
- Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or furrow
- Destroy infected plant material — do NOT compost
- Resistant varieties: Tylka F1, Roma VF (some tolerance)

### 2. Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum)

**Symptoms:** Sudden complete wilting of entire plant with green leaves (no yellowing). Brown discoloration of stem vascular tissue (cut stem and place in water — milky threads visible). Often kills plant within days of first symptom.

**No cure once infected.** Control through prevention:
- Use resistant varieties: Anna F1, Cal-J (intermediate resistance)
- Crop rotation: do NOT plant tomatoes/potatoes/eggplant in infested soil for 3+ years
- Drench transplants with Copper Hydroxide (Kocide) before transplanting
- Remove and destroy wilted plants immediately
- Solarize soil (cover with clear plastic for 4–6 weeks during hot season)

### 3. Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)

**Symptoms:** Young leaves cup upward and inward; leaves yellow and have a leathery texture; severe stunting; flowers fall; very little or no fruit set.

**Vector:** Bemisia tabaci (silverleaf/sweet potato whitefly). Transmitted within minutes.

**Control:**
- Use resistant varieties: Tylka F1, Kilele F1 (TYLCV resistance listed by seed company)
- Control whitefly: Yellow sticky traps; Imidacloprid (Confidor) systemic spray; Spirotetramat (Movento)
- Reflective mulches reduce whitefly landing
- Remove and destroy infected plants
- Do NOT transplant near older tomato crops

### 4. Blossom End Rot (BER)

Not a disease — a calcium deficiency disorder.

**Symptoms:** Dark, leathery, sunken area at blossom end (tip) of fruit.

**Cause:** Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, usually caused by irregular irrigation (drought stress followed by over-watering) rather than lack of soil calcium.

**Treatment:** Maintain consistent irrigation; foliar spray of calcium chloride (5g/L) every 7–10 days during fruiting.
content_sw:
## Magonjwa Makuu ya Nyanya Afrika Mashariki

### 1. Kuoza kwa Majani (Late Blight)

Dalili: madoa ya maji kwenye majani yanayogeuka kahawia-nyeusi. Inasambaa haraka sana hali ya unyevunyevu na baridi.

Tiba: Mancozeb (Dithane M45) kila siku 7–10; Ridomil Gold kama dalili zimeanza.

### 2. Kunyauka kwa Bakteria (Bacterial Wilt)

Dalili: Mmea unanyauka ghafla na majani bado ya kijani. Hakuna tiba — zuia kwa aina zinazostahimili na mzunguko wa mazao.

### 3. Virusi ya TYLCV

Dalili: Majani mapya yanajipinda na kugeuka njano; mmea unakuwa mfupi. Inasambazwa na nzi weupe.

Tiba: Tumia aina zinazostahimili (Tylka F1); dhibiti nzi weupe.

title: Cereal Stem Borers — Maize, Sorghum, Millet Management
content:
## Cereal Stem Borers in East Africa

Two major stem borer species affect maize, sorghum, and millet:

1. **African Stem Borer** (Busseola fusca) — highland areas (>1000m), cool temperatures
2. **Spotted Stem Borer** (Chilo partellus) — lowland/mid-altitude, invasive from Asia

### Symptoms

- **Young plants:** 'Dead heart' — central leaf turns yellow-brown and dies. Pull it out: it comes away easily
- **Older plants:** Entry holes in stem; frass (grain-like excrement) at entry point; weakened stems that break easily ('lodging')
- **Cob stage:** Borer attacks cob, allowing fungal infection

### Economic threshold

Spray when >10% of plants show fresh dead hearts (V1–V6 stage).

### Control

**Chemical:**
- Carbofuran granules (Furadan 3G): apply 1–2 granules into whorl — effective but toxic; handle with care
- Lambda-cyhalothrin (Karate): 300ml/ha into whorl
- Emamectin benzoate (Coragen): 200ml/ha

**Biological:**
- Trichogramma egg parasitoid: release 50,000 parasitoids/ha at egg-laying stage
- Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt): spray into whorl; less effective against older larvae
- Push-Pull intercropping: plant Desmodium between maize rows + Napier grass border — repels borers, attracts parasitoids; very effective long-term strategy promoted by ICIPE
